## Highlights

- **Security fix:** the browser no longer spell-checks the secrets typed into Tale's credential fields, such as the API keys, tokens and passwords under **Settings › Connectors** and **Settings › AI providers**, and the credentials under **Settings › Data residency** and **Settings › Enterprise SSO**. These fields are text fields drawn as dots, and the browser treated them as text. Before this release, a browser with enhanced spell checking turned on, such as Chrome with **Enhanced spell check** or Edge with Microsoft Editor, could send what was typed there to its spell-check service, and a phone's keyboard could capitalize or correct it. The fields now turn spell checking, capitalization and correction off, as the browser does for a password field. Sign-in and account passwords are real password fields and were not affected. See the upgrade notes.
- An integration that mirrors conversations into the Inbox through the [API](https://docs.tale.dev/develop/api-reference#mirror-conversations-and-deliver-replies) keeps them when its key is replaced. A mirrored conversation now belongs to whom the key belongs to, not to the key itself. Before this release, a new key made for a team or the organization was refused with `INTEGRATION_NOT_OWNED` (403) for every conversation the old key had mirrored, and the replies queued for those conversations were stranded. The new key now continues those mirrors, lists them and claims the replies queued before the swap. A personal key, and a key an Owner or Admin made for a member, act as that person, as before, and a key that belongs to someone else is still refused. An upload stays with the key that staged it, so a new key stages its own attachments. Two keys made for the same team or the organization now share their mirrors: see the upgrade notes ([#5007](https://github.com/tale-project/tale/issues/5007)).
- Under **Settings › Data residency › Knowledge database**, [**Test connection**](https://docs.tale.dev/self-hosted/configuration/data-residency#connect-an-organizations-knowledge-database) now follows the TLS rules of Tale's own connections to the database. Before this release, the test fell back to an unencrypted connection under the SSL mode `prefer`, which those connections never do. So a database without TLS passed the test, Tale's connections to it then failed, and a later save of another embedding model was refused. Under `verify-ca` and `verify-full` the test ignored `POSTGRES_CA_FILE`, and under `verify-ca` it also checked the server's name. So a server whose certificate a private CA signed failed the test, although Tale's connections to it worked. The test now requires TLS under `prefer`, checks the certificate against `POSTGRES_CA_FILE` but not the server's name under `verify-ca`, and checks both under `verify-full`. See the upgrade notes ([#5330](https://github.com/tale-project/tale/issues/5330)).
- Uploading a file no longer gets slower with every upload in an organization whose file storage refuses to delete files. Each upload also tidies up the organization's expired uploads. Before this release, it went through all of them every time, so while the storage refused to delete them, they piled up and each upload took longer than the one before. It now takes at most 25 of them per upload, oldest first. Two sends that attach the same files in opposite orders at the same time, such as two emails sent through a connector or two replies queued through the API, no longer deadlock, which failed one of them with a server error (see [#4208](https://github.com/tale-project/tale/issues/4208)).
- The [Session Manager](https://github.com/tale-project/tale/blob/main/services/session-manager/README.md), new in this release, runs isolated browser sessions on your own computer ([#5332](https://github.com/tale-project/tale/pull/5332)):
  - Each session is a Camoufox browser (an anti-detect Firefox) with its own profile, its own stable fingerprint and its own proxy, so no two sessions share cookies, storage or an IP address. You see and use the browsers in a web page, keep the logins, cards and notes you type into pages again and again in its **Secrets** section, and can let an AI assistant use everything through MCP.
  - It is for one person on their own machine, for testing, research or managing accounts. It has no accounts and no login, so its [security model](https://github.com/tale-project/tale/blob/main/services/session-manager/README.md#security-model) is about who can reach its address:
    - it listens on `127.0.0.1` only;
    - it answers only requests that address it by its own name and port, which blocks DNS rebinding;
    - it refuses every change that another origin sends, and its API, its MCP endpoint and its live view refuse any request that another site, or another origin on this computer, starts;
    - AI access is off until the person at the page switches it on: a connected assistant can use every session and read every secret, passwords and card numbers included;
    - a browser does not inherit the secrets in the app's environment, and the app's answers carry no proxy password, except the proxy export.
  - It keeps proxy passwords and secrets in plain text in its database, readable by every program that runs as you, so protect them as you protect the disk. It sends nothing to Tale or to any analytics service.
  - This release publishes it as the image `ghcr.io/tale-project/tale/tale-session-manager:0.5.98`, with the Compose file `compose.session-manager.yml` at the root of the repository. Nothing in a Tale deployment starts it: `compose.yml` and `tale deploy` leave it out.

## Upgrade notes

- At start, the backend applies the migration `0235_conversation_api_source_owners.sql`:
  - It adds the columns `owner_principal_kind` and `owner_principal_id` to `app.conversation_api_bindings`, which record whom each API-mirrored conversation belongs to.
  - It fills them for the existing rows. A mirror that a key made for a team or the organization created belongs to that team or organization, and every other mirror belongs to its user, as before.
  - A trigger fills them for the rows that the previous image inserts during a rolling deploy.
  - Until every platform image runs this release, the previous image still refuses a replacement key, so replace a team's or the organization's key after the roll.
- Keys made for the same team or the organization are now one integration: each of them lists, changes and claims the mirrors that any of them created. Before this release, Tale kept two integrations that ran on two such keys apart. If two of yours mirror under the same `source`, a claim by either now also takes the replies queued for the other's conversations. To keep integrations apart, give each its own team or member, as the [API reference](https://docs.tale.dev/develop/api-reference#mirror-conversations-and-deliver-replies) says; the mirrors they created before the upgrade stay with their team or organization.
- The API contract stays at `3.52.0`.
- **Test connection** under the SSL mode `prefer` now fails for a knowledge database that serves no TLS, as Tale's connections to it already did. Turn TLS on in that database, or choose `disable` when it is reachable only over a network you trust. With `POSTGRES_CA_FILE` set, the test now reads that file under every SSL mode but `disable`, as Tale's connections do, and fails when the backend cannot read it. The connections themselves are unchanged.
- The Session Manager asks nothing of an operator who does not run it. To run it in Docker, follow [its README](https://github.com/tale-project/tale/blob/main/services/session-manager/README.md#run-it-in-docker):
  - From the root of a checkout of this release, run `PULL_POLICY=always VERSION=0.5.98 docker compose -f compose.session-manager.yml up -d`. It pulls this release's image, publishes it on `127.0.0.1:3004` and keeps its data in the volume `session-manager-data`. Without `PULL_POLICY=always`, Compose builds the image from the checkout instead.
  - Keep the port on `127.0.0.1`: whoever reaches it can open every session, read the secrets and drive the browsers. To reach it from another machine, put a reverse proxy that authenticates in front of it, and list the address people use, `host:port` as the address bar shows it, in `SESSION_MANAGER_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, together with `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` on its port, which a value replaces.
  - The first start downloads the browser, a GeoIP database and the uBlock Origin add-on, about 700 MB, which unpack to about 1.26 GB in the volume. The GeoIP database and the add-on come without a checksum. Give the container 2 GB of memory, and 3 GB when `/tmp` is a tmpfs.
  - In the container the browsers have no WebGL, which sites can see: when the fingerprint's fidelity matters, run it natively with Bun, as the README's quick start says. The image for `arm64` is built but not yet verified.
  - It rebuilds an earlier Python app from a separate repository, and does not take over that app's data.
- If people typed credentials into the fields of the security fix above with enhanced spell checking on, and your policy treats text sent to a browser's spell-check service as disclosed, rotate those credentials.
- No configuration, limit, credential or sign-in setting needs to change beyond these: the other fixes take effect with the new images.
